We are grateful to Reviewer kH4W for detailed comments on our work, as well as for the positive assessment of the empirical study covering a comprehensive battery of memory tasks and theoretical analysis.

> W1, W2. Although the motivation is clear, it seems like the performance of RATE relied heavily on previously introduced memory embeddings and cached hidden states, as shown in the ablation study RQ1. This raises a question about the degree of novelty and contribution of the MRV component itself versus inherited advantages from prior architectures. 

Thank you for the remark. While RATE builds on earlier memory-augmented transformers, its contribution lies in integrating segment-level recurrence, learnable memory embeddings, and the MRV mechanism, and in demonstrating that this combination is necessary for reliable long-horizon behavior in sparse POMDPs. Prior models were developed for single-modality NLP, whereas RATE is designed for heterogeneous offline RL trajectories (observations, actions, returns-to-go) and provides a formal guarantee on memory preservation through MRV. Our ablations show that neither recurrence alone, nor cached states, nor gating mechanisms can maintain sparse cues over thousands of steps; only the full architecture does so, and direct adaptations of RMT or TrXL fall short of RATE on ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, and Minigrid-Memory.

> W3. Minor: The paper is quite dense, which makes some figures difficult to read due to the small font and cramped layout. While the inclusion of many experiments is commendable, improving figure clarity would help accessibility. In Figure 5, the y-axis label at 0.0 overlaps with the x-axis tick at 〖10〗^1. Slightly adjusting the axis limits or label offsets may resolve this issue.

We thank the Reviewer for pointing this out. We have corrected the axis overlap in Figure 5 and improved font size and spacing across all figures. The updated .pdf paper now uses adjusted axis limits and label offsets to ensure readability.

> W4. Minor: The authors could include one or two sentences explaining what is meant by “cached hidden states”, as this is not a widely standardized term. Providing a brief description in the main text (rather than requiring readers to refer back to the original paper) would improve readability and self-containment.

In the revised manuscript, we now include a brief inline definition of “cached hidden states” at first mention. We clarify that the term refers to transformer activations from previous segments that are stored and reused as additional keys and values during attention, thereby extending effective context length without reprocessing earlier tokens (please, see L157-161).

We are grateful to Reviewer xQWj for comments on our work, as well as for acknowledging the comprehensive experimental coverage and the presence of a theoretical component.

> W1, W4. Incremental novelty. RATE mainly extends prior memory-augmented transformers (RMT, TrXL, Compressive Transformer) by combining existing mechanisms; MRV, while effective, is a variant of cross-attention gating rather than a fundamentally new idea; 

Thank you for the comment. RATE is indeed built on prior memory transformers, but its novelty comes from combining segment-level recurrence, learned memory embeddings, and MRV, and showing that this combination is required for stable long-horizon performance in sparse POMDPs. Unlike RMT, TrXL, and Compressive Transformer, designed for single-modality NLP, RATE handles heterogeneous offline RL trajectories (observations, actions, returns-to-go) and introduces MRV with a provable memory preservation bound. Ablations confirm that neither RMT-style recurrence, nor cached states, nor gating alone is sufficient to retain sparse cues over thousands of steps; only the full design succeeds, and direct RMT/TrXL adaptations underperform RATE in ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, and Minigrid-Memory tasks.

> W2. Theoretical analysis scope. The preservation theorem bounds norm differences but does not connect to RL performance or convergence guarantees, limiting theoretical depth.

Theorem 1 is not meant to provide full RL performance guarantees, but to formalize a key property of MRV: it prevents memory from being overwritten. In sparse, long-horizon tasks, this is necessary for good policy performance, and our ablations confirm that removing this property leads to failure. Extending the analysis would require stronger assumptions about policy learning and offline RL dynamics, which we view as promising future work.

> W3. Computational and scaling costs. The paper does not quantify the runtime or memory overhead of segment recurrence and MRV compared with DT or RMT, which is crucial for practical adoption.
Q1. How large is the compute/memory overhead of MRV and recurrent caching relative to standard DT or RMT during training and inference?

Decision Transformer (DT) serves as the primary baseline, since RATE extends its architecture. This makes DT the most direct reference point for assessing the effect of adding memory mechanisms.

Appendix, Table 13 reports practical compute metrics: training time per epoch, per-step inference latency, and GPU memory usage, while Table 12 lists parameter counts, showing that RATE remains efficient relative to DT.

For instance, in the T-Maze setting, RATE achieves markedly higher performance than DT:
| Metric| RATE | DT | Relative Difference |
|-|-|--|-|
| Training time per epoch| 16.17 ± 2.75 s        | 95.75 ± 0.49 s        | ~5.9x faster |
| Inference latency per step| 7.20 ± 0.31 ms        | 10.69 ± 0.14 ms       | ~33% lower |
| GPU memory footprint  | 3.148 MiB   | 8.608 MiB        | ~63% lower|
| Number of parameters   | 1,723,840    | 1,775,488 |~2.91% fewer|

These results show that RATE not only improves long-horizon memory performance but also delivers concrete efficiency benefits in speed and resource usage.


> W5. Lack of reference: It is noted that this paper compare their method with "Decision Mamba". However, there is another existing work which also adopts mamba as its backbone [1].

Thanks for the notion! We've added the Decision Mamba by Lv, Qi, et al. to the Related Work section and also added as a baseline to the experiments on MuJoCo (Table 3). We also duplicate the results here (for the DT, RATE, DMamba by Ota T., and DMamba by Lv, Qi, et al.). Thus, we see that RATE, developed not for solving MDP control tasks, but for memory-intensive POMDP tasks, shows comparable performance to SOTA SSM-based models on such MDP control tasks, demonstrating its versatility:

| M | Walker2d | 74.0±1.4 | 80.7±0.7 | 78.2±0.6 | 80.3±0.07 |
| MR | HalfCheetah | 36.6±0.8 | 39.0±0.6 | 39.6±0.1 | 40.8±0.43 |

We did not experiment with DMamba by Lv, Qi, et al. on our memory-intensive tasks, as we could not find open-source code implementing this model. However, based on the paper, it is likely that this model, like DT or DMamba by Ota T., is incapable of solving memory-intensive tasks with memory horizons longer than the context length. However, DMamba by Lv, Qi, et al. provides more precise control over the MDP tasks.

summary.value: This paper introduces RATE (Recurrent Action Transformer with Memory), a transformer-based architecture for offline reinforcement learning (RL) that explicitly integrates memory mechanisms to improve performance in partially observable and long-horizon tasks. RATE processes trajectories in segments and passes information between them through memory embeddings, cached hidden states, and a novel Memory Retention Valve (MRV)—a cross-attention module controlling what information to retain or overwrite. The authors provide a theoretical bound guaranteeing partial memory preservation between updates and show strong results across memory-intensive environments (T-Maze, ViZDoom-Two-Colors, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory, POPGym) while remaining competitive on standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks. Extensive ablations isolate the contributions of MRV and memory embeddings and demonstrate RATE’s robustness in sparse, long-horizon POMDPs.

strengths.value:
- Strong motivation and clear contribution. The paper identifies a concrete weakness of Decision Transformer (DT)—limited context for long-term dependencies—and addresses it with a principled, integrated memory mechanism rather than ad hoc recurrence.

- Theoretical component. Theorem 1 provides a nontrivial formal result bounding memory preservation under α-alignment, adding rigor beyond empirical evidence.

- Comprehensive experimental coverage. RATE is evaluated on a wide spectrum of domains, from classic MDPs to highly memory-dependent tasks, showing consistent advantages and strong extrapolation (up to 9600 steps in T-Maze).

weaknesses.value:
- Incremental novelty. RATE mainly extends prior memory-augmented transformers (RMT, TrXL, Compressive Transformer) by combining existing mechanisms; MRV, while effective, is a variant of cross-attention gating rather than a fundamentally new idea.

- Theoretical analysis scope. The preservation theorem bounds norm differences but does not connect to RL performance or convergence guarantees, limiting theoretical depth.

- Computational and scaling costs. The paper does not quantify the runtime or memory overhead of segment recurrence and MRV compared with DT or RMT, which is crucial for practical adoption.

- Conceptual overlap with existing work. RATE’s motivation and mechanism strongly resemble RMT (2022) with an added gating step; the paper could better articulate its distinct advantages and design rationale.

- Lack of reference: It is noted that this paper compare their method with "Decision Mamba". However, there is another existing work which also adopts mamba as its backbone [1].

[1] Lv, Qi, et al. "Decision mamba: A multi-grained state space model with self-evolution regularization for offline RL." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 22827-22849.

comment.value:
We sincerely appreciate the Reviewers’ thoughtful feedback and their recognition of RATE as a principled and effective memory-augmented transformer architecture for offline RL in long-horizon, partially observable environments. Their comments affirm the contributions of our work, and we are pleased that they find the motivation, theoretical grounding, and empirical evaluation meaningful. Below, we summarize the key strengths highlighted in the reviews:

1. **Clear motivation and principled architectural design.** Addressing the concrete limitation of Decision Transformers in handling long-term dependencies through a well-motivated, integrated hybrid memory mechanism (Reviewers xQWj, kH4W, o12m).

2. **Strong theoretical component.** Providing a memory-preservation bound under $\alpha$-alignment and offering useful analytical insight into the behavior of the Memory Retention Valve (Reviewers xQWj, kH4W).

3. **Extensive and well-executed empirical evaluation.** Demonstrating strong performance across a broad suite of memory-intensive POMDPs (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory, 48 POPGym tasks) and standard MDP tasks (Atari, MuJoCo) with consistent long-horizon advantages (Reviewers o12m, xQWj, kH4W).

4. **Extensive ablation studies.** Including noise-based component ablations, gating-variant comparisons, and analyses of memory embeddings and cached hidden states, which clearly isolate the contributions of each module in RATE (Reviewers o12m, tfiE).

5. **Clarity and useful visual explanations.** Such as the T-Maze illustration in Figure 2, which Reviewers noted as a clear depiction of how RATE and DT differ in their handling of memory cues (Reviewer tfiE).

We again thank all Reviewers for their time, careful evaluations, and constructive comments. Across the rebuttal, we focused on four main concerns: 

1. Clarifying the presentation of RATE and the MRV, including improved figures, notation, and Algorithm 1; 

2. Disentangling the specific contribution of MRV relative to learned memory embeddings and cached hidden states, and explaining why the full combination is necessary for long-horizon POMDPs; 

3. Quantifying the computational overhead and showing that segment-level recurrence yields concrete efficiency gains relative to DT despite the added modules; and 

4. Strengthening comparisons and positioning with respect to related sequence models, including TrXL, RMT, Decision Mamba, Reinformer, and Elastic DT, and explaining why trajectory stitching cannot account for the observed failures on memory-intensive tasks.

We believe these revisions have substantially improved the presentation of the paper, clarifying RATE’s positioning, architecture, and empirical analysis. We are grateful for the Reviewers’ engagement and are confident that the updated paper addresses all of the concerns they raised.

summary.value: This paper introduces the Recurrent Action Transformer with Memory (RATE), a transformer-based architecture for offline reinforcement learning (RL) in partially observable and memory-intensive environments. RATE incorporates three memory mechanisms includinlearned memory embeddings, recurrent caching of hidden states, and the Memory Retention Valve (MRV), a cross-attention module designed for selective retention of key information across long sequences. The method is evaluated on a diverse suite of tasks, including ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Minigrid-Memory, Memory Maze, POPGym, as well as Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks. Experimental results and ablation studies are provided, alongside theoretical analysis on memory preservation by the MRV.

summary.value:
The authors focus on solving POMDPs using transformers, in offline RL scenarios. They propose the Recurrent Action Transformer with Memory (RATE), which implements various modules described below. In particular, the authors focus on efficiently processing long contexts.

The proposed Memory Retention Valve (MRV) allows information to flow between sliding attention windows. Normal transformers are $O(n^2)$ space complexity, where $n$ is the length of the trajectory. However, by integrating recurrence through the memory retention valve, one can decouple $n$ from the trajectory length. 

The proposed method breaks a trajectory into fixed-length, non-overlapping segments. Memory tokens $M$ span these fixed-length segments, enabling context beyond the sliding window. Each segment goes through self attention to produce embedding tokens $S$. I will admit it is not entirely clear to me what happens next. It appears that the current memory tokens $M$ for the segment $n$ are concatenated twice to either end of the current embedding tokens $S$ (Algorithm 1, line 6). But these are all initialized to 0 (Algorithm 1 line 3).

The authors go on to prove how quickly inputs vanish through the MRV. To do so, they make the assumptions that the rows of each memory token $M$ are $ell_2$-normalized. I will admit the proof was a bit difficult to follow and I did not check it thoroughly.

Finally, the authors compare their method to more standard models such as the Decision Transformer, Transformer XL, Decision Mamba, GRU, and LSTM. They perform significant evaluation and analysis on T-Maze and related tasks, finding that the proposed method achieves state of the art results. They report similar results on Minigrid and POPGym baselines. 

Finally, they perform ablations on their model by replacing various memory model components with random noise. They perform an upper-bound estimate by turning POMDPs into MDPs and training the Decision Transformers on them. Finally, they provide ablation for various gating mechanisms for the MRV.

strengths.value:
Transformers struggle with long contexts, and in RL this is especially painful due to poor sample efficiency. Introducing recurrence into a transformer is a good way to fix this issue.

In general, the authors provide a good amount of evidence for their method. They compare against other memory models and even training algorithms. Critically, they compare against TrXL which is similar to their method. They provide ablations for each part of their proposed method, and even test different gating methods for the MRV.

We thank Reviewer 012m for the detailed assessment. We appreciate the acknowledgment of the central contributions, in particular the integration of recurrence into transformer-based RL agents to address long-context limitations. We also value the recognition of the breadth of the empirical study, including comparisons against diverse memory architectures and training schemes, as well as ablations that isolate each component of the approach and an evaluation of multiple MRV gating mechanisms.

We have revised the manuscript to address the comments on figure quality and exposition (see blue text). We further note that no concerns were raised regarding correctness, novelty, empirical rigor, or significance, which constitute the primary ICLR evaluation criteria. All points of criticism pertain solely to presentation, and no technical issues or missing results were identified.

**Regarding to summary:**
> current memory tokens … are concatenated twice … But these are all initialized to 0 (Algorithm 1 line 3).

The memory tokens are initialized not by zeros, but by random vectors from a normal distribution (Algorithm 1, line 3). As shown in Algorithm 1, this initialization occurs once before processing the first segment in the sequence, not before processing each segment.

> They perform significant evaluation and analysis on T-Maze and related tasks. … They report similar results on Minigrid and POPGym baselines

We would like to point out that our evaluations are not limited to the "T-Maze and Related Tasks" and Minigrid and POPGym benchmarks. We consider a wide range of different tasks with different action and observation spaces, different reward functions, different time horizons, and different memory usage scenarios: T-Maze, ViZDoom-Two-Colors, Memory Maze, the POPGym suite of 48 different memory puzzles and POMDP control tasks. We also tested the proposed model on a specially designed Action Associative Retrieval task (Appendix, D) and on various MDP game and control environments (Atari and MuJoCo). Thus, our evaluations cover a very wide range of different problem classes.

> Finally, they perform ablations on their model by replacing various memory model components with random noise. They perform an upper-bound estimate by turning POMDPs into MDPs and training the Decision Transformers on them. Finally, they provide ablation for various gating mechanisms for the MRV.

Please note that the main text only presents the basic ablation studies, while the Appendix contains extended ablations examining various components of the RATE model (Appendix: Figures 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22).

**Weaknesses:**

> W1. Figure 1 is too blurry and small to read, even after zooming to the maximum allowed

Figure 1 may not be too blurry, as it is uploaded as a full-resolution .pdf file using vector graphics. However, we have increased its size in the updated text (see pdf file).

> W2. Experimental setup and results in the approach (section 3, lines 131-139) seem misplaced

The purpose of this paragraph, followed by reference to Figure 2 (L148), is to provide a high-level demonstration of the difference between RATE and DT, in order to improve understanding of the subsequent detailed description of the proposed model.

> W3. The text surrounding the MRV is difficult to understand (lines 141-160, algorithm 1)

Regarding your comment on the notation of MRV inputs and outputs: we meant that MRV takes $M_n$ and $M_{n+1}$ as inputs and returns an updated value for $M_{n+1}$, which we reflected through the assignment operator ($\leftarrow$), which is typical for pseudocode. To make the description of our model more accessible, we updated the text for Section 3, where we describe our method in more detail. We would also like to point out that a diagram of how exactly the memory embedding is updated was already present in the paper and is available in the Appendix, Figure 15.

If you have any other specific comments about the text, we would appreciate it if you would mention them during the discussion so that we can improve our understanding of our work.

> W4. Section 3.1 is jarring and also a bit difficult to read, I think it should be moved to the appendix

We believe the proof is a central component of the contribution and plays a critical role in understanding the theoretical claims, so we prefer to keep it in the main text. We would appreciate clarification on what aspects you found “jarring and also a bit difficult to read” to help us revise the presentation and improve its accessibility.

**Questions:**

> Q2. Can MRV’s gating dynamics be visualized—e.g., which segments’ information it chooses to retain or forget?

Thanks for the suggestion! We will add the visualization to the Appendix in the updated .pdf file of the paper.

> Q3. How sensitive is performance to the number of memory tokens m and segment length K?

The short answer: even adding a single memory token significantly improves model performance compared to using no memory tokens at all. A few memory embeddings (5-15) are sufficient to achieve optimal performance. Dividing sequences into 3-9 training-length segments (depending on available computing power) also proves most reliable. However, it's important to keep in mind that the optimal segment size ensures that the information being remembered and the moment of its use are not in the same segment, in order to foster learning memory. For more detailed results, see the ablation study in the Appendix, Figures 13, 14, and 18.

> Q4. How does RATE behave under noisy or corrupted observation sequences beyond the artificial noise ablation?

Our experiments on POPGym included POMDP control tasks, where random noise was used to add noise to certain components of the observation vector (NoisyPositionOnlyCartPole, NoisyPositionOnlyPendulum) or to completely disable them (PositionOnlyCartPole, PositionOnlyPendulum, VelocityOnlyCartPole) - see Appendix, Table 9. On these tasks, RATE shows results close to the dataset average return, confirming its robustness to these types of tasks.

Furthermore, experiments on MuJoCo tasks (Table 3) can also be viewed as experiments with noisy data, where the dataset contains suboptimal trajectories with poor/random actions. In these experiments, RATE also demonstrates performance comparable to or better than baselines developed specifically for this type of task, further confirming RATE's ability to handle noisy or corrupted observation sequences.

We have revised the manuscript to improve clarity (see the highlighted in blue changes in the updated version). 

Overall, we want to once again thank Reviewer xQWj for their efforts and thoughtful feedback, and hope that our responses have helped clarify the contributions of our work. We are happy to answer additional questions during the discussion to further improve the accessibility of our work.

We are grateful to Reviewer tfiE for their feedback on our work. In particular, we appreciate the Reviewer's appreciation of our experiments and ablation studies.

> Q1. Minors: The algorithm 1 can be clearer in term of describing the outputs. The output of the algorithm 1 is inside the for loop.

In the original notation, we meant that after processing each segment within the for loop, we obtain the predicted action values ​​for that segment to calculate the loss, as well as an updated value for memory embeddings. We acknowledge that the current version of Algorithm 1 may prompt further questions, so we have revised it accordingly (see the attached .pdf containing the updated paper text).

We are once again grateful to Reviewer tfiE for their time and effort in contributing to our work.

title.value: Second part of the Authors Comment

comment.value:
> Q1. The Decision Transformer (DT) underperformance on memory-dependent tasks such as T-Maze may stem not from memory limitations, but rather from its lack of trajectory stitching ability; that is, its inability to combine underperforming trajectories into coherent long-horizon trajectories. In cases where underperforming trajectories are more frequent than successful ones, DT will often follow the underperforming paths, further degrading performance. The results would be more convincing if the authors compared against (applying on top of) more advanced DT architectures, such as Reinformer [1] or Elastic DT (EDT) [2], which explicitly address the trajectory stitching issue.

We thank the Reviewer for raising the trajectory-stitching hypothesis and for pointing us to Reinformer and Elastic DT. However, the T-Maze and ViZDoom-Two-Colors results cannot be explained by stitching limitations. Instead, they are driven by a lack of long-horizon memory. 

In all T-Maze experiments, the training dataset contains only trajectories from an optimal policy with 100% success rate. Therefore, there is no distributional imbalance between successful and failed rollouts and no need to recombine prefixes across episodes. Any trajectory-stitching failure mode is therefore structurally absent.

Additionally, as shown in Figure 6, DT achieves perfect performance when the cue lies inside the attention window and collapses to ~50% success (random guessing) as soon as the cue moves beyond it. This degradation occurs despite all trajectories being optimal, confirming that the bottleneck is long-range memory retention, not return-based trajectory composition.

Reinformer and Elastic DT address a different failure mode (value recombination across suboptimal trajectories), but do not provide a mechanism for preserving observation-level information over thousands of steps. They could in principle be combined with RATE, and we agree they are interesting complementary directions. We have therefore added both works to the Related Work section and will discuss how stitching and memory issues differ in their failure signatures.

In addition, the trajectory stitching hypothesis is incompatible with the structure of memory-intensive tasks such as ViZDoom-Two-Colors. In standard MDP settings, stitching can improve coverage by combining high-value prefixes and suffixes across trajectories. In ViZDoom-Two-Colors, however, the decisive information is a single early observation that specifies which object type must be collected. Trajectories with different pillar colors correspond to distinct conditional policies, and mixing fragments across them destroys the required mapping from early cues to later actions. Under these conditions, models that explicitly encourage stitching can be misled by superficially similar but semantically incompatible trajectory fragments. As you requested, we have added Elastic DT (EDT) as an additional baseline in our experiments, as well as referenced both papers you mentioned in the revised text. Consistent with the task structure described above, EDT performs substantially worse than both DT and RATE, supporting the conclusion that trajectory stitching is not the source of DT’s failure on these memory-dependent tasks:

| Method     | Total        | Red          | Green         |
|------------|--------------|--------------|----------------|
| RATE       | 59.21±1.19   | 57.38±1.15   | 60.77±2.14     |
| DT         | 31.45±1.21   | 14.56±0.90   | 48.35±3.23     |
| Elastic-DT | 5.28±0.18    | 5.25±0.15    | 5.33±0.22      |

Elastic-DT is negatively affected by the heterogeneity of trajectories associated with different pillar colors, since its stitching mechanism encourages the model to treat red and green episodes as recombinable, even though they encode incompatible dependencies. This failure mode further supports our claim that the dominant bottleneck in these tasks is long-range memory retention rather than trajectory recomposition.

> Q2. In Table 13, RATE includes extra components such as MRV and memory embeddings, yet it often shows lower training time, inference latency, and GPU memory usage compared to DT. Could the authors clarify why adding these components does not increase computational cost, and how RATE achieves higher efficiency despite the additional modules?

A comparison of RATE and DT in terms of training time per epoch, inference latency per step, and GPU memory footprint, as well as the number of parameters, can be found in Appendix, Tables 12 and 13.

For instance, in the T-Maze setting, RATE achieves markedly higher performance than DT:
| Metric | RATE| DT| Rel. Diff.|
|-|-|-|-|
| Training time per epoch   | 16.17 ± 2.75 s | 95.75 ± 0.49 s    |~5.9x faster|
| Inference latency per step| 7.20 ± 0.31 ms        | 10.69 ± 0.14 ms |~33% lower|
| GPU memory footprint      | 3.148 MiB             | 8.608 MiB| ~63% lower|
| Number of parameters      | 1,723,840             | 1,775,488 | ~2.91% fewer

These results show that RATE not only improves long-horizon memory performance but also delivers concrete efficiency benefits in speed and resource usage. Key reason - segment-level recurrence reduces attention complexity (RATE process the trajectory in $N=T/K$ segments of length $K$ instead of full sequence $T$). Additionally, MRV cost is negligible relative to multi-head attention, since MRV is a single lightweight cross-attention over $m\times m$ tensors, where $m$ ~ $10^0$.

We have revised the manuscript to improve clarity (see the highlighted in blue changes in the updated version). 

We are once again grateful to the Reviewer kH4W for their detailed comments on our work. We are open to further discussion and will be happy to answer any other questions about our work.

comment.value:
**Questions:**

> Q1. Can you explain what static recurrence means here?

By "static recurrence" we mean recurrence where the recurrent state is not updated by the model (no gates, no memory evolution). We've added an explanation of this term in the updated text (please, see L210-213).


> Q2. What is "alignment" referring to here?

In our work, the term “alignment” refers only to a geometric notion. Two vectors are called “$\alpha$-aligned” when the angle between them is at most a given threshold $\alpha$, meaning that the vectors point in similar directions. We use this notion to formalize stability properties of the memory update, (please, see L213-215). It is entirely unrelated to “alignment” in the sense of preference tuning or behavioral alignment used in the context of LLMs.

> Q3. Is this a bug? Should it be concat(M_n, S_n, M_{n+1})?

No, this isn't a bug; it's a feature of causal self-attention (see L149: "each segment is prepended and appended with memory embeddings").
We attach the same memory embeddings $M_n$ to the beginning and end of the corresponding segment $S_n$ due to causal masking used in the transformer decoder. Using two copies gives read access (every token in the segment can attend back to memory) from pre-memory embeddings, and write access (memory tokens appear after segment content, enabling the final layer to attend forward into segment embeddings) from post-memory embeddings. If only the prefix existed, memory would only be read, never updated; if only the suffix existed, the segment could not use memory. We have added a more detailed explanation in L168-173.

> Q4. I know is $\leftarrow$ assignment but what does $\rightarrow$ mean here?

It is a mathematical shorthand for “is fed into / is used to compute” the loss. In other words, the notation means: “The predicted action $\hat{a}_n$​ is passed into the loss function $\mathcal{L}(a_n,\hat{a}_n).”

> Q5. How are you returning from inside a for-loop at each iteration? Is this a generator?

No, this is not a generator, and there is no return happening inside the loop.
The pseudocode is written in algorithmic notation, not an imperative programming language. The loop continues normally until all segments have been processed. Then there is a transition to the next batch and so on.

We have revised the manuscript to improve clarity (see the highlighted in blue changes in the updated version). We also refined the layout of Figures 1-8 and Tables 1-6 to enhance readability.

We once again thank Reviewer 012m for their comments. We also want to reiterate that all of Reviewer 012m's comments relate solely to the text formatting, not to the methodological or experimental components. We have taken into account all of the reviewer's comments regarding the text formatting and updated the attached .pdf file with the article (see blue text).

We also ask the Reviewer to be more specific and concrete, and to clarify what they meant by "this is not an exhaustive list but just some representative example" and "Section 3.1 is jarring and also a bit difficult to read" during the discussion, so that we can make our text more accessible. This is especially important to us, as Reviewer 012m writes, "I cannot recommend acceptance without a substantial rewrite," while limiting themself to only general comments on the text and illustrations.

summary.value: The paper proposes the Recurrent Action Transformer with Memory (RATE) to address partial observability in offline RL. The reviewers universally acknowledged the extensive empirical evaluation and the method's superior performance on memory-intensive tasks compared to strong baselines. While initial concerns regarding presentation and incremental novelty were raised, the rebuttal effectively demonstrated that RATE offers significant computational advantages (faster than DT) and that alternative hypotheses (e.g., trajectory stitching) do not explain the performance gains. Given the technical soundness acknowledged even by the most critical reviewer and the comprehensive rebuttal addressing efficiency and baselines, the paper is recommended for acceptance.
